doc.title: Buddy Burns and Frank Pasley Interview, 1968-09-23

title: Naming the Dirty Dozens blues
summary: Burns says his blues was nameless but kids called it the Dirty Dozens.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: And this blues you played before, do you have a name for it?
Well, I never named, that's my own too. No name, just the blues? Yeah, yeah, blues. We used to call them the Dirty Blues, the Dirty Dozens. Dirty Dozens.
Oh yeah. Can you play that? Can you play that one, the Dirty Dozens?
I just played it. Oh, that was the one you played? Yeah, yeah, that's what we used to call it. We was young kids, you know, we just give it
that name, you know. Can you still remember this Buster Anderson blues? Buster Anderson, let's see. Let me see. What's the name?

Something like your blues? Huh? Something like your blues, Mr. Clay, huh? Oh, that's, what's it called? Rebs, that's, that's, uh, Reynes, Reynes, old chords. You remember Reynes. Let me see how you... Jam it to hell. Cher I can't play that damn thing the most. I used to go play the heck out of that. That sound good, too. What's the Anderson Blues, what is? No, this is Ernest O'Cos. What's the Anderson Blues? Ernest O'Cos? O'Cos, yeah. He's dead a long time, too. Played piano. Played quite a few dirty blues, you know.
